title: Maximus' good cheer
hookLine: from Maximus: self-command, cheerfulness in illness, doing duties without complaint (Meditations 1.15)

lines: THE ONE WHO MAKES THE ROOM LIGHTER.
cards: Some people can't empty the dishwasher without a soundtrack of sighs. Others just do it.

And now and then you meet someone who does the dull job, the hard job, even the job they're too sick for, and somehow makes the room lighter while they do it. What lingers is less what they said than the air around them.
Marcus had a friend like that, a senator and Stoic named Claudius Maximus, and gave him a long, detailed portrait in book one.

teach.b: First, who he was. Claudius Maximus was a Roman senator and a Stoic.
He governed the province of Africa, and history happens to remember him as the judge at a well-known trial there, where the writer Apuleius was accused of using magic to win a rich wife.
Apuleius's speech in his own defense still survives. Second, the portrait. From Maximus, Marcus says, he learned to govern himself and not be pushed off course by anything.
To be cheerful in every circumstance, illnesses included. To mix gentleness and dignity in the right measure.

teach.h: NO RUSH, NO DELAY, NO FAKE LAUGH.
teach.b: And to do the work in front of him without complaining. Third, the details. Everyone believed Maximus meant what he said, and that whatever he did, he did without bad intent.
He never seemed astonished or rattled, never rushed, never put things off, never lost heart, and never laughed to cover up irritation. He was quick to do good and quick to forgive.
And a lovely line: nobody ever felt looked down on by Maximus, and nobody ever dared think himself better than him. Fourth, cheer without complaint. The two sit together.
Complaint is often the sound of carrying something while making sure everyone knows how heavy it is.

teach.h: CARRY IT, KEEP THE WEIGHT QUIET.
teach.b: Maximus carried it and kept the weight to himself, so the people around him could breathe easier.
Later in the notebook, Marcus writes simply that Maximus died. Book one keeps him as Marcus saw him: doing the job in front of him, cheerfully, without a word about how hard it was.

how: Some readers of the Meditations take Maximus as a model for doing tedious or hard tasks steadily and without complaint, especially when tired or unwell.

games.q: you're Maximus, unwell, with a full day of duties in the province. what do you do?
o: cancel everything and let people know why.
do the work, cheerfully, without complaint.
do it, but make sure everyone hears how sick you are.
games.why: Marcus remembers him as cheerful in illness, doing what was set before him without complaining.

practice: Think of one duty waiting for you that you'd usually grumble about: the laundry, the expense report, the call you've been dodging.
Picture doing it the way Maximus might have, not grinning falsely, just steady and unhurried, without the sighs, and notice what changes for the people near you.

wordCard.voice: Claudius Maximus. The Roman senator and Stoic who did his duties without complaint, cheerful even in illness, so no one near him felt small. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: no complaint. Carry it, and keep the weight of it quiet. Until tomorrow.
